newsitem.title: ISRAEL: 'Free Vanunu' campaign comes to Israel.
newsitem.headline: 'Free Vanunu' campaign comes to Israel.

text.p: "I am happy for revealing what I revealed."
The message, signed Mordechai Vanunu, was read on Monday to the first conference in Israel called to demand the release of the nuclear technician most Israelis still brand a traitor.
Actress Susannah York read the one line smuggled out of the prison where Vanunu has spent 10 years in solitary confinement since being lured from London in a Mossad honeytrap.
Nobel peace laureate Joseph Rotblat, who worked with Robert Oppenhemimer on the first atomic bomb, appealed to Israel to free Vanunu.

"Vanunu is not a traitor but a whistleblower," Rotblat said. He said Vanunu's 18-year sentence was out of proportion to his crime. He was jailed for giving details of Israel's nuclear programme to the London Sunday Times.
Rotblat opened the two-day conference which included international scientists, lawyers and human rights activists.

Participants talked openly about Vanunu and the nuclear arsenal Israel has never acknowledged having. The gathering was unprecedented in Israel where Vanunu is still vilified as a spy and where nuclear issues are shrouded by official censorship.
"This is a landmark in the Vanunu affair," Vanunu's brother, Meir Vanunu, told Reuters.
"The fact that we can talk about the kidnapping openly is significant. The fact that (Israeli) papers are allowed, yes allowed, to write a lot more freely about it shows a change," Meir Vanunu said.

Meir Vanunu, who returned to Israel this year after seven years in Britain campaigning for his brother's release, said he faced an uphill task changing the attitude of Israelis, particularly that of Shimon Peres.
Peres was prime minister in 1986 when the Mossad secret service learned that Vanunu had passed on information about the Dimona nuclear complex.

It sent a woman agent codenamed Cindy to lure Vanunu from Britain. Israel did not want to jeopardise its relations with then Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher by operating on British soil. Vanunu flew to Rome with Cindy where he was kidnapped by Israeli agents, drugged and spirited back to the Jewish state. His family did not know what had happened to him for six weeks.

Vanunu wrote the date of his abduction on the palm of his hand which he pressed against a police car window for photographers when being taken to court. Cindy has been identified by the Sunday Times as a U.S. citizen living in Israel.

Rotblat said Vanunu did no significant harm to Israel's nuclear programme. Rotblat said Vanunu disagreed with Israel's policy of hiding the existence of its nuclear weapons which he wanted made public.

Rotblat said a spy like Klaus Fuchs, who sent Moscow details of the Nagasaki bomb, endangered security by giving information secretly to a "brutal regime". Vanunu revealed what he knew openly, without payment, because he believed in the cause of peace, Rotblat said. Fuchs served nine years of a 14-year sentence.
It's an argument lost on his fellow Nobel peace prize winner Peres.
"I thought that no single person can decide the fate of a nation," Peres told Reuters in an interview in August when asked if he had dealt fairly with Vanunu.
"He is a spy. Nobody in England or in America would support this sort of a story," Peres said.

Delegates at the conference said Israel should show Vanunu the same concern as Jonathan Pollard. Israelis are pressing the United States to free Pollard, an American Jew who stole U.S. naval secrets for Israel.

Meir Vanunu said Israeli public opinion had not yet turned around. He expected his brother to remain in jail for at least the next two years, although he hoped that Mordechai would be freed from solitary confinement.

Former right-wing Israeli cabinet minister Yuval Ne'eman, a physics professor who was involved in Israel's nuclear project from the start, told Reuters on Monday: "I think that from the point of view of the endangering of the future of the state of Israel, Vanunu committed an act that in other countries might have been punished with death."
